title: Yunmen's one word
hookLine: the master remembered for answering in one word

cards: A monk has been saving up a question. It is big, the kind you ask a great teacher once. He bows, and asks: what is the teaching that goes beyond all the Buddhas and all the ancestors?
The hall goes quiet. The teacher, Yunmen, answers with one word. Cake.

Not a parable, not a sermon. A sesame cake, an everyday snack. Yunmen was a Chan teacher in southern China, and his students remembered him for answers like that: so short they stop you in the doorway.

teach.b: First, the collections. Yunmen's replies were gathered by his students and later set into the koan collections, among them the Blue Cliff Record, where the cake exchange appears.
Some readers speak of his one-word barriers: a single word, set across the path like a gate you have to pass through, not walk around. Second, another one.

teach.h: WHAT IS BUDDHA? A DRIED STICK.
teach.b: In the Gateless Gate, a monk asks him, what is Buddha? And Yunmen answers with the name of a dried stick, the plain kind once kept in the outhouse. It sounds rude.
It is meant to. The monk was holding Buddha up high and far away, and Yunmen dropped it right into the most ordinary corner of the house. Third, what the one word does.
A long answer gives the mind something to chew on, and the chewing can go on forever.

teach.h: ONE WORD GIVES THE MIND NOWHERE TO GO.
teach.b: One word gives it nowhere to go. Cake. The question that seemed so grand meets a small, real thing you could buy and eat today.
Teachers say the point is not the cake, but what happens in the listener the instant the long thinking stops. Fourth, the cost. One word is easy to say and hard to mean.
Yunmen's answers came from long practice, and his students took them away to sit with, sometimes for a long time.

teach.h: SHORT IS NOT THE SAME AS QUICK.
teach.b: Short, here, is not the same as quick.

how: Yunmen's replies appear in koan collections such as the Blue Cliff Record and the Gateless Gate, which Zen students work with in meditation and in private meetings with a teacher.

o: a Chan teacher well-known for his one-word answers
a Chinese pastry offered at temple feasts
a gate at the entrance of a Chan monastery

games.q: Yunmen's one word: tap the pairs.
p: a gate you must pass through

s: Yunmen's short answers were meant as insults to the Buddha
the dried stick brought Buddha out of the clouds and into the ordinary house.
his replies were gathered into koan collections
the Blue Cliff Record and the Gateless Gate both carry them.
a one-word answer was meant to be quick and easy
students sat with these words, sometimes for a long time.

games.q: you're Yunmen. a monk asks, with great seriousness, what is the teaching that goes beyond all the Buddhas and ancestors? what do you say?
o: give a long talk on the teaching
tell him the question is too advanced
games.why: Yunmen said cake: a plain sesame cake. the grand question meets a small, real thing, and the long thinking has nowhere to go.

practice: Ask yourself quietly, what is here right now, and let one word come instead of a sentence: warm, tired, traffic, breath.
Breathe with that one word, and when the explaining starts up, the because and the but, let it fall away; if a new word arrives, let it replace the old one.

wordCard.voice: Yunmen. The Chan teacher whose short replies, cake, a dried stick, cut his students' long questions short. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one word. Easy to say, and hard to mean. Day nine hundred ninety-one, done.
